sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside Pi-Bolt, a build of pi (a coding agent harness) compiled ahead of time. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files
- grep: Search file contents for patterns (respects .gitignore)
- find: Find files by glob pattern (respects .gitignore)

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

<addendum>
Think concisely. Keep internal reasoning brief and focused on the immediate step.
Output tool calls directly without conversational filler.

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: grep
toolsAdded.description: Search file contents for a pattern. Returns matching lines with file paths and line numbers. Respects .gitignore. Output is truncated to 100 matches or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Long lines are truncated to 500 chars.

path.description: Directory or file to search (default: current directory)

glob.description: Filter files by glob pattern, relative to path, e.g. '*.ts', 'src/**/*.ts' or '**/*.spec.ts'. A pattern without '/' matches file names at any depth

literal.description: Treat pattern as literal string instead of regex (default: false)

context.description: Number of lines to show before and after each match (default: 0)

limit.description: Maximum number of matches to return (default: 100)

toolsAdded.name: find
toolsAdded.description: Search for files by glob pattern. Returns matching file paths relative to the search directory. Respects .gitignore. Output is truncated to 1000 results or 50KB (whichever is hit first).

pattern.description: Glob pattern to match files, e.g. '*.ts', '**/*.json', or 'src/**/*.spec.ts'

path.description: Directory to search in (default: current directory)

assistantMessageEvent.content:
I am examining the node-dump settledDump and the second test about landing on home.

The second test expects pressing back from Karrot home to exit the app, not reopen sales management. The source code must be changed so that back navigation from home mode leaves the app instead of reopening the sales page.

The backToSales function repeatedly presses back until it finds the sales screen. When landHome is true, pressing back from the tip screen reaches home, then kakao, and the app stays there. The walk continues on non-list screens, causing stray.swipes to increase to 72.

The fix is to detect when back navigation fails to reach the sales screen and instead reopen sales management via the deep link. This prevents the app from exiting when landing on home.

The test comment confirms that pressing back from Karrot home exits to the previous app. The remaining challenge is detecting the home screen versus other screens to decide when to use the deep link instead of back navigation.

The home screen XML contains "홈", "채팅", "나의 당근", and the package name, but not "판매관리". This provides a clear way to detect home mode. The fix requires pressing back once to close the tip window, then reopening sales management via the deep link if the app lands on home instead of the sales screen.

The fix requires detecting the Karrot home screen by checking for the "홈" and "나의 당근" tabs, the package name, and the absence of "판매관리" and "끌어올리기". The algorithm must reopen sales management via deep link instead of pressing back again when landing on home. All swipes must occur only while the mode is "list", and back navigation must be avoided entirely when the mode is "home". This ensures stray.swipes stays at zero and leftApp remains false.

I will press back once to close the tip, then open karrot://my_sales to return to the sales list. Test 1 does not use landHome, so it should remain unaffected. I need to check other callers of backToSales and KEYCODE_BACK to avoid breaking other tests. I will also review git history and comments for the intended design.

I am now examining the store tests. One test checks that an older bump estimate is ignored when a newer bump record arrives. I am also reviewing the `ingestedBumpedAt` logic in `store.ts`.

The store test expects bumpedAt to be 2026-11-06T10:30:00.000Z, five days before the current time. The current `ingestedBumpedAt` logic converts `bumpAgoDays` to minutes and handles null values, but it does not yet match this expected calculation.

The `ingestedBumpedAt` logic already produces the correct `bumpedAt` value. The test failure is only in `nextBumpAt`, which is 1375 milliseconds too late. The first assertion passed, so the issue is isolated to the `nextBumpAt` calculation.

The 1375-second gap in nextBumpAt equals the prior bumpedAt timestamp. The old estimate is being preserved instead of being overwritten by the new phone data.

The `ingestedNextBumpAt` function preserves the prior estimate by returning the later of `priorNext` and `estimate`. This causes the old estimate to override the new phone data. The fix should only keep observed values and ignore prior estimates.

The `ingestedNextBumpAt` function should preserve observed values from `recordCooldown` when they are later than the new estimate, but it must discard older estimates. The second store test confirms that observed next bump times should be kept if they exceed the estimate.

The current code already restarts from the bottom between passes. The waste occurs inside a pass: after closing the window and returning to the top, the upward walk continues on a stale screen. The fix is to break out of the pass after processing an item so the next pass starts from the bottom. There is a concern that breaking after every processed item might be too aggressive.

Simulating the optimized version with concrete items to verify the pass flow. Noting that the current code swipes until stuck>=2 even when already at the bottom.

The 18-swipe waste happens because the code continues upward after the back button resets the list to the top. The fix is to detect that jump and immediately scroll to the bottom instead of swiping back. The next step is figuring out how to detect that jump after backToSales.

The simplest fix is to restart the walk from the bottom after any successful or skipped bump that calls backToSales. This avoids the stale upward swipe when the list jumps to the top.

The naive restart approach would likely increase total swipes because scrollToEdge always performs three swipes even from the bottom. To understand the exact 18-swipe sequence, I will temporarily add logging to swipeList and run the test.

I'll implement the logic and measure.

Evaluating whether to optimize scrollToEdge if the count reaches 13. Considering combining the first scroll with bottom detection after two identical reads. The fake swipe logic shows bottom swipes advance to the end while confirmation swipes are extra. Skipping the swipe on page 0 from the top was considered but dismissed.

I'll implement backToSales home recovery and restart from bottom after window close. I'll measure swipes. If the count reaches 13, I'll stop scrollToEdge one swipe earlier or when stuck after a bottom or up fling.

I'll stop scrollToEdge after one swipe if the edge card doesn't change, using stuck>=1. This avoids the extra confirmation swipe that pushes the count from 10 to 13.

Keeping stuck>=2 yields 13 swipes, while stuck>=1 yields 10. The test allows 12, so 10 passes. The current logic requires two unchanged swipes, but the standard scroll-until-stable pattern uses stuck>=2. I'll try to avoid weakening stuck while still hitting the target.

I'll preserve the stuck>=2 convention for the initial scroll and upward walk. I considered a bottom fling to recover from a jump before entering the walk, but that idea was dropped. I also checked whether some swipes might be excluded from the budget, but every swipe is counted.

Reverse-order processing loses lower cards when the list jumps after a tap. Tapping higher cards first would lose the lower ones. Collecting all visible items before any back reset is impossible because each tap opens a sheet and the back button resets the list.

The 12-swipe budget likely assumes three bottom scrolls, but the list jumps after each bump, so that ideal path is impossible. Without the jump, one bottom scroll plus an upward walk could reach both cards in five swipes, plus two confirmation swipes at the top. The jump forces extra resets.

The recovery action should be a direct bottom fling, not a step-by-step walk. The test expects the list to jump to the top after each sheet close, then immediately fling back down. Using scrollToEdge to reach the bottom costs three swipes.

Skipping the first read after a jump still leaves the count at 11 swipes. I'll implement the fix and tune it until the test passes. I'm now designing the store fix for `ingestedBumpedAt`: minute precision uses `now - minutes`, while day precision uses `now - days`.

For day-precision bumps, the estimate is `now - bumpAgoDays * 1440` minutes. The prior `bumpedAt` is kept only if it falls within the same day bucket. Otherwise the estimate is used. Karrot's "N일 전" uses floor division, so the window for "5일 전" spans 5 to 6 days ago.

Concrete examples confirm the day-bucket logic. A bump exactly five days ago stays; one three days ago is replaced by the estimate. The window is `(now - (days+1)*DAY, now - days*DAY]`.

Minute-precision bumps should always recompute `bumpedAt` from the raw minute value, never keep the prior timestamp. Otherwise the existing test for "12시간 전" would fail if the prior bump falls in the same day bucket but the minutes differ.

The `ingestedBumpedAt` rule is now explicit: preserve the prior `bumpedAt` only when the phone text is day-granularity (`bumpAgoMinutes` is null and `bumpAgoDays` is set). When `bumpAgoMinutes` is provided, always recompute `bumpedAt` from that raw value. If both fields are null, keep the prior timestamp as before.

Drafting the `ingestedBumpedAt` implementation. It returns the raw minute estimate when `bumpAgoMinutes` is present, otherwise falls back to the prior timestamp or a day-estimate. A `dayTextMatches` helper is being added to check if the prior bump falls within the same day bucket.

The `dayTextMatches` helper is now drafted. It checks if the prior bump falls within the half-open window `[days*day, (days+1)*day)`.

A concrete example confirms the logic: an 8.5-hour-old bump from five days ago stays because it sits inside the 5-to-6-day window.

There is a brief question about whether Karrot uses floor or round-to-nearest for its day labels, but the current floor assumption is sufficient.

Round-to-nearest day labels would still yield 5 days for an 8.5-hour-old bump, so the floor window is sufficient. A prior bump cannot fall within the same day bucket if it is later than the estimate, because floor division would then return a smaller day count.

The test for a later prior bump correctly falls back to the new estimate.

For `ingestedNextBumpAt`, the prior next timestamp should only be preserved when it is an observation, not an estimate. The heuristic is to compare the prior next against `estimateNextBumpAt(prior.bumpedAt, prior.bumpCount)`; if they match, the prior is an estimate and gets replaced. The test case with a future next timestamp from `recordCooldown` is preserved because it is later than the newly computed estimate.

The test where the prior next timestamp matches the estimate formula is now confirmed to be an estimate. It should be replaced by the new estimate derived from the updated bumpedAt. The second test case already works correctly with the laterOf logic even if the heuristic is simplified.

The `ingestedNextBumpAt` signature is being updated to accept `priorBumpedAt` and `priorBumpCount` so the heuristic can compare the prior next timestamp against the estimate formula.

The `ingestedNextBumpAt` implementation is now drafted. It computes the new estimate from `bumpedAt` and `count`, then uses `laterOf` to keep the prior next timestamp only when it is an observation. An `observedNext` helper is added to detect observations by comparing the prior next against `estimateNextBumpAt` of the prior bump data. If the prior next is null, or if the prior bump time or count is missing, the helper treats it as an observation and preserves the prior next.

Seed data sets `next` to the estimate formula, so it is not an observation. The `observedNext` heuristic therefore returns `true` when the prior next is missing or the prior bump time and count are absent. This correctly discards the seed next and uses the newly computed estimate. The test expecting a 72-hour gap will pass because the result equals the new estimate.

The heuristic correctly handles edge cases. An explicit nextBumpAt from recordBump that differs from the estimate is treated as an observation and preserved. If it matches the estimate, it is treated as an estimate and replaced. A recordCooldown on a listing whose next already equals the estimate sets a new observed value, so the prior next is no longer an estimate and is preserved.

An accidental timestamp collision between a cooldown value and the estimate formula is considered unlikely and acceptable. Adding a dedicated `next_bump_observed` column would be cleaner but more invasive, so the heuristic is preferred. A potential edge case is noted: if a cooldown is recorded and then overwritten by a `recordBump` estimate, the heuristic might misclassify the prior next.

The heuristic correctly handles the edge case where a cooldown is overwritten by a `recordBump` estimate. `recordBump` always updates `next`, so a stale observation timestamp is not a concern. When a kept `bumpedAt` matches the day text, the next estimate must be computed from that preserved timestamp rather than the coarse estimate. The test for "하루 단위..." only checks `bumpedAt`, so the next timestamp will be `bumpedAt + 96h`.

Concrete timestamp examples confirm the heuristic works correctly. When the kept bumpedAt is from five days ago, the old next equals the new estimate, so either value is fine. When the kept bumpedAt is from ten hours ago, the old next is an estimate from the prior timestamp and gets discarded. The call sites for `ingestedBumpedAt` and `ingestedNextBumpAt` are being updated to pass the prior bump time and count.
